cases.catches: A granted, implemented declared member reaching the host and answering ok: any regression in policy binding, member dispatch or the ok branch turns a successful run into an exit-65 diagnostic.
The second member of the same family runs under the same grant: a dispatcher keyed only to the first member name would fail this case.
Dropping `--capability-policy` must fail closed before a host is built: a build that silently falls back to deny_all or to allow_all would show a different exit or a missing diagnostic.
A policy file that is not JSON must be refused, never ignored: a reader that treats a parse failure as an empty grant list would run the program.
A policy may authorize only members the toolchain serves: granting demo.echo@0.1.0.say must be refused at binding, not accepted and then answered by nobody.
A grant is per member, not per family: granting scalar_count must not authorize concat, and the refusal must reach the adapter (exit 65, capability failure).
A member the registry does not declare must be rejected at graph check: a checker that trusts the call spelling over the declaration would let an unknown name reach the host.
An argument the declaration does not name must be rejected, never dropped: a decoder that ignores extra named arguments would still run the call.
Passing fewer arguments than the declaration requires must be rejected before the host, not filled in with defaults the declaration never stated.
A well-formed literal of the wrong declared type must be rejected at graph check and the diagnostic must name both types: a checker that only compares arity would pass this program to the host.
A host refusal after dispatch reaches the VM: the two 40,000-byte arguments exceed the 65,536-byte declared text budget, so the run must end 65 with a capability fault rather than a status 0.
cases.program:
re 0.1 compact

unit @declared

cap @strings: revia.strings@0.1.0

fn @main() -> process.status {
  %r = @strings.concat(left: "", right: "")
  return match %r {
    ok(_) => process.exit(0)
    err(_) => process.exit(1)
  }
}

cases.catches: A registry artifact carrying another schema identifier must be refused as a registry error: accepting it would let an unrelated document define host members.

A registry may not carry an error family that no member names: the round trip from declaration to host shape must not depend on an entry nothing references, so a reader that keeps unused types would doctor host capability from an unreachable table.
Two declarations of the same reference must be refused, not merged or decided by order: a reader that silently keeps the last one would make host shape depend on document order.
